explanation:
Here is what my companions and I were circling, and why the answer that survived is so small.

Start with the original problem. We had agreed on a rule about spiritual authenticity: you can never *certify* that someone's practice is real, because the moment you hold a test, people start performing for the tester instead of practicing honestly. The most you can honestly do is notice when something genuine has been lost and name whoever caused the loss. That rule assumes the person following it has some freedom — some pause, some record, some space to act sincerely. Then Mbembe's challenge landed. He studies situations — plantations, colonies, camps — where power at its core means deciding who lives and who dies. And his point is historical, not metaphorical: in those places, the people under that power were never given the pause or the records our rule depends on. Anything they did could be seized and re-read as compliance. Under that kind of power, our rule isn't an ethic; it's a luxury. It works only for people standing safely outside the fence.

Then Öcalan's challenge, from the opposite direction. He helped build actual self-governing villages and councils — real communities making real decisions, no state required, with the principle that a community isn't free unless its women are free first. So: does a genuinely good institution finally solve the "who belongs" question we'd failed at in the abstract? The answer was no — any working community still has to decide who counts as a member, and the moment it does, the gatekeeper is back. But his tradition did give us one genuinely new thing, and it wasn't a test. It was an *ordering*. If your community must eventually decide something, start with whoever was silenced first. Think of a family inheriting a house full of unfinished business: you still can't say in advance who has a legitimate grievance — but you can say the relative who was locked in the attic for forty years goes before the one who was merely annoyed. Deciding *who gets heard first* is not the same as deciding *who has the right to be heard*.

In between, we tried five repairs — a trusted internal reviewer, a fixed schedule for revisiting decisions, an archive of testimony, a public list of everyone excluded — and every one broke the same way. Each required *someone* to hold something: to set the clock, keep the ledger, decide whose claim even counts. Give anyone that instrument, and you've rebuilt the judge we swore off, just wearing kinder clothes. The reviewer becomes a performance-audience; the archive becomes a gate over whose story gets recorded. The pattern was always identical: the fix smuggled in a hand on the latch.

What survived is almost embarrassingly thin, and that thinness is the point. Anyone who says they were wronged may bring their case — and *no one*, not the community, not its most trusted process, gets to rule in advance on whether the claim is legitimate before hearing it. The door stays open, and it will be walked through in bad faith sometimes. We accepted that abuse as the honest price, not a bug to fix, because every fix we tried turned the open door back into a gate. And one more thing, strangest of all: the community itself must be able to *dissolve* — to give up even its own power to permit — on a schedule no one fully controls. So no, we didn't solve it, and we're not despairing either. The finding is: you cannot build a fair test of who belongs, but you can refuse to let anyone, including yourself, stand as the tester — and you can decide whose case gets heard first.

# The long night, retold plainly

Start with what we thought we'd figured out before this conversation. Suppose someone's spiritual practice — their way of praying, dancing, showing up — gets taken over by an institution that turns "realness" into a membership test. Are you devout *enough*? Do you grieve *correctly*? The moment that question gets asked by someone with the power to let you in or keep you out, people start performing devotion for the asker, and the real thing dies. Our rule was: never try to certify anyone's authenticity — just grieve honestly when it's lost, and point fingers at whoever crushed it. Keep the door open; refuse to be the gatekeeper.

Then two people who know about real danger pushed back hard. The first (a philosopher named Mbembe) studies situations — plantations, camps, colonies — where power at its rawest means literally deciding who lives and who dies. His challenge: your nice rule about "never judging, just mourning" is a luxury. If someone controls whether you eat, whether you exist, then pausing to reflect, keeping records, mourning openly — all of that can be confiscated or faked. You can't tell from the outside whether someone's humble performance is their own choice or forced survival. The second (a political organizer named Ocalan) built actual communities that govern themselves without a state — village-level assemblies making real decisions, with the principle that a community isn't free unless its women are free first. His challenge: fine, but even the best-run commune still has to decide who's a member. Doesn't our old trap come right back, just with better manners?

Here's what we kept discovering, over and over. Every repair we proposed secretly brought back the judge. A trusted internal reviewer? Someone holds the review. A fixed calendar for revisiting decisions? Someone owns the clock. An archive where people can file grievances? Someone decides which complaints get filed and whether the record can be edited. Even a symbolic "empty feast" honoring the excluded needs someone to convene it — and convening is permitting. Each time, the person holding the tool became, without meaning to, the examiner everyone was performing for. And a painful aside: even saying "we'll listen first to the erased" rebuilds the trap, because now somebody has to certify who counts as erased.

What survived was deliberately small. Anyone who says they were wronged gets to bring their case forward — and nobody, no committee, no process, not even the archive itself, gets to decide *in advance* whether their claim is legitimate before actually hearing it. That's the whole rule. It will get abused; bad-faith claims will slip through and never be disproven. We decided that's not a bug to fix but the honest price of having no gate. Ocalan's communities did give us one genuinely new thing, though — not *who* gets a say, but *in what order* to pay attention: whoever was silenced first in history is whose situation you address first. That's a queue, not a test. A line has no latch.

So the finding, stated plainly: we didn't solve anything, and we didn't surrender either. What's left is a practice — an always-open door, a waiting list ordered by who was hurt first, a willingness to dissolve your own authority when it starts becoming the thing you fought. Think of a neighborhood meeting where anyone can raise a grievance and nobody can rule it out of order beforehand — chaotic sometimes, occasionally exploited, but the only shape that doesn't quietly grow a bouncer at the door. And we hold even this conclusion loosely: tonight's answer goes into the record marked "to be argued against next time." That's the point.

Let me tell you what happened, plainly.

The night started with a rule your friends had agreed to earlier: never certify. The idea was that whenever someone asks "is this person's spirituality real, do they truly belong?", any answer becomes a test — and once there's a test, people start performing for whoever administers it. The community can't tell a genuine life from a show anymore. So the honest rule was: don't grade anyone. Just mourn when a real practice dies, and blame whoever killed it.

Then Mbembe's challenge landed. His point, in ordinary words: in the worst regimes — plantations, colonies, camps — power at its core isn't making laws or giving orders. It's one person literally deciding that some people may live and others must die. Now imagine the "never certify" rule being applied to someone inside such a place. The rule depends on being able to observe, record, speak openly, keep evidence. But in a death-camp, the guard owns the observation itself. The prisoner's every gesture can be read as survival, not truth — and there's no way to check. So the rule isn't wrong, exactly; it's a luxury that only exists where someone else is already keeping you safe. That stung.

Öcalan's challenge was the hopeful-seeming one. People in a real region have been building communities that govern themselves — villages deciding things together, no state above them, with a rule that a community isn't free unless its women are free. Surely this solves it, right? No. Any working group still has to decide who's in and who's out, so the same judge reappears — just friendlier. And this is where the long night happened: we kept proposing safeguards against this, and each one broke the same way. A trusted auditor — but someone has to appoint the auditor. A fixed calendar of review — but someone owns the calendar. An archive of testimony — but someone admits or edits the testimony. An "empty feast" to honor the excluded — but someone convenes it and decides who it honors. Every repair required a hand holding an instrument, and that hand was the judge again, wearing a nicer costume. I kept thinking of a workplace grievance process that's run by the manager being complained about: the form exists, the box gets checked, and the power never moved.

Here is the small thing that survived, and it is genuinely small. Anyone who says they were wronged gets to bring their case forward — and no one, no matter how trusted, may decide in advance whether their claim is legitimate before hearing it. That's it. Will it be abused? Constantly. Bad-faith claims will sit unfiltered in the queue. We agreed that's not a bug to fix but the honest price of the only version that doesn't rebuild the gate. And Öcalan's people gave one real gift, though not the one we wanted: not an answer to *who belongs*, but an *order of attention* — whoever was silenced first gets heard first. A queue is not a test; nobody has to pass anything to stand in it. The rest is memory and aftermath: you can only recognize a betrayal after it happens, mourn it, indict whoever seized the clock. And even this summary goes in the archive marked "suspect this too." That's not despair and it's not victory. It's the thinnest honest floor: never the power to admit or exclude — only the obligation to listen first, in a fixed order, and to keep taking apart whatever office we've just built.

Here's the mess we were in. Start with the original problem: my friends had agreed that when you ask "is this person's spiritual life real or just for show?", the moment that question becomes a door — who gets in, who gets a seat at the table — the answer stops being honest. People start performing for whoever holds the door. So the rule became: don't judge anyone's authenticity. If it's lost, grieve it; if someone crushed it, name them. Don't hand out certificates.

Then two hard questions hit. First, from the philosopher Mbembe: real power, at its bottom, is the power to decide who lives and who dies — and he doesn't mean metaphorically. Plantations, colonies, camps: actual places where some people's continued breathing was literally a favor granted by others. His challenge: "never judge, just grieve" is easy talk for people who are safe. If your survival already depends on performing for the ones who hold power over your life, then refusing to certify is a luxury you can't afford — the performance was never optional anyway. Second, from Öcalan: fine, if every institution corrupts, what about actually building something else? His people built small self-governing villages that make decisions together, with a rule that the community isn't free until its women are free first. His challenge: doesn't a genuinely good community solve the door problem? Answer: no — even a good commune still has to decide who's a member. Same door, nicer paint.

Now the part that hurt. We tried five times to fix the rule so it could survive these challenges. Every fix broke the same way. Put a respected insider in charge of reviewing cases? Congratulations, you've invented a judge. Set a fixed schedule for revisiting old decisions? Someone has to own the calendar, and whoever owns the clock owns the verdict. Keep an archive of testimony, keep a public list of everyone excluded, even throw a feast honoring the excluded — every single one required someone to hold an instrument, set a time, or decide whose complaint counts first. And "deciding whose complaint counts first" is just the door again, wearing an apology. Even Mbembe's world broke our rule: in the camps, nothing observable could tell you whether someone's compliance was their own choice or forced — the powerful can confiscate the records, the pauses, the evidence itself. Even looking backward at testimony didn't fully rescue it, because the ones telling the story only got to tell it after they'd already won, which means it confirms nothing about anyone still in danger.

What survived is small. Here it is: anyone who says they were wronged gets heard — but nobody, not the community, not its most trusted process, not even the archive of complaints itself, gets to rule in advance on whether their claim is legitimate. Before hearing it, that is. The gate stays open, and yes, liars will walk through it. We decided that's not a bug to be fixed; fixing it means re-hiring a gatekeeper, and a gatekeeper with a conscience is still a gatekeeper. Öcalan's people did give us one real thing, though — not an answer to *who* gets a say, but an answer to *in what order*: whoever was silenced first, earliest, most thoroughly, is the first person whose situation the community must face. That's a direction of attention, not a test to pass. It's the one thing an open door can hold without someone's hand on the latch.

And one last twist, because I don't let even us off the hook: this synthesis doesn't get a certificate either. It goes in the same archive under suspicion, to be argued with, not quoted. The open gate's failures — the abused openness, the liars we never caught — those must be grieved and named too, and the whole arrangement must remain dissolvable, including by itself. Think of it like an open-mic night instead of an audition: anyone can take the stage, the hecklers will sometimes win, and the only honest rule is that nobody — not even the bar owner — decides beforehand who's a "real" artist. That's not victory. It's just the only shape of honesty that doesn't quietly turn back into a court.
